# Publishing and following live composition drafts

A live draft is an explicit, playable snapshot—not the contents of a file halfway through a write. Publish after each coherent phrase or section (often 4–8 bars across all parts), and again after meaningful revisions. Do not wait for a whole movement or sonata if an earlier section is already listenable.

## One-time conventions

- Reserve a stable work ID, for example `bach-violin-sonata-1`, and an existing composing request, for example `bach:violin-sonata:1`.
- The normal completed-work catalogue does not contain drafts. The draft service derives composer, form and round from the request and exposes snapshots separately.
- Scores remain owned by the composing agent. Infrastructure agents must not change the music.
- Keep private working files and raw session histories outside the public repository. Public change notes should be short, high-level descriptions of what changed, not private internal reasoning or unreviewed chat exports.

## Create a descriptor

Keep a descriptor in the composition workspace. Paths are relative to the descriptor file, not to the shell's current directory:

```json
{
  "id": "bach-violin-sonata-1",
  "requestId": "bach:violin-sonata:1",
  "title": "Bach’s Missing Violin Sonata",
  "subtitle": "Sonata in E minor for violin and keyboard",
  "description": "Original AI-composed homage; work in progress.",
  "movements": [
    {
      "id": "i",
      "label": "I. Adagio",
      "file": "../missing-works/scores/bach-violin-sonata-1-i.abc",
      "note": "Opening phrase, bars 1–8."
    }
  ]
}
```

Supply every movement that should be in this snapshot. Do not include nonexistent or unplayable movements. Movement IDs must stay stable as the work grows, so a listener following movement II remains on II when a new revision arrives. A later snapshot may have more movements or more bars; it may also revise earlier music.

## Publish

From the source checkout:

```sh
node tools/publish-draft.mjs \
  --manifest earlier-workspace/draft.json \
  --message "Added the opening imitation; revised the bass in bars 5–8." \
  --expect 0
```

The first expected revision is 0. For the next publish use the previous returned revision, or omit `--expect` if you deliberately want to publish against whatever is latest. An expected-revision mismatch prevents an older writer from accidentally replacing a newer take. `--dry-run` validates without publishing.

The command reads the `.abc` files and sends a structured payload over SSH stdin to the owner-only publishing CLI. It does not put score text or metadata into a shell command. Public visitors cannot upload or replace drafts.

The server validates syntax, matching parts and complete bars before publishing. This is **not** a verdict on harmony, counterpoint, instrumental practicality, or musical quality. Those remain the composer's responsibility. Invalid snapshots leave the previous playable draft unchanged.

Successful publication returns a revision number and a listening link:

`https://lost-compositions.exe.xyz/work.html?draft=bach-violin-sonata-1`

## What listeners see

- A clearly labelled draft with its revision, publication time, change note, available movements and bar counts.
- While stopped and following latest, new snapshots appear automatically.
- While playing, loading, paused, or editing the source locally, the score and audio remain on the current take. A new-version notice offers an explicit switch.
- Switching stops the old take; an update never starts playback on its own. The listener can choose a starting bar or click a note after switching. The bar navigator counts a pickup as its first written bar; published progress counts exclude pickups. The control states this convention, and repeated bars use their first occurrence.
- A revision selector opens older takes. Returning to Follow latest resumes updates.
- A network failure leaves the last playable take visible. The page retries without silently replacing it with partial data.

The draft page checks for updates while it is open and visible. This is browser refresh behavior, not an agent generation schedule.

## Completing the work

Follow `docs/composing.md`: publish the finished catalogue entry and its score/notebook/transcript files, synchronize the server catalogue, then complete the request through the SSH-only admin CLI. Do not mark it completed merely because a draft has been published.

The draft viewer will link to the finished work, and its revision history remains accessible. If the request is reopened, its existing snapshots stay available but are labelled as paused rather than actively composing.

## Storage and deployment

Snapshots live under `/var/lib/missing-works/drafts`, separate from `/var/www/missing-works/releases`. Routine website releases cannot delete the history. Public read routes serve only validated metadata and score files, never arbitrary local files. Do not copy the private snapshot state into the static public file list.

This directory persists across service restarts. Existing automated backups cover the vote database; off-host archival of draft history is not automatic. Treat the scores in the composition workspace and source repository as additional copies, not a substitute for an archive backup policy.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Expand a .mw source (blocks, transposed reuse) and compile it to ABC.
usage: build.py stem [outfile]
Directives (each on its own comment line):
  % @DEF name        start recording a block (the block is also emitted where it is defined)
  % @END             stop recording
  % @USE name [iv]   emit the block again, transposed by an interval such as +P4, -M2, +m3, +P8, 0
  % @HIDE / % @SHOW  skip the lines in between (unfinished material kept out of the build)
"""
import pathlib, subprocess, sys, re
ROOT = pathlib.Path('workspace/')
IV = {'P1': (0, 0), 'm2': (1, 1), 'M2': (1, 2), 'm3': (2, 3), 'M3': (2, 4), 'P4': (3, 5), 'A4': (3, 6), 'd5': (4, 6), 'P5': (4, 7),
      'm6': (5, 8), 'M6': (5, 9), 'm7': (6, 10), 'M7': (6, 11), 'P8': (7, 12)}
LET = 'CDEFGAB'; SEMI = [0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11]
def tr_note(acc, letter, octs, d, s):
    up = letter.upper(); o = (4 if letter == up else 5) + octs.count("'") - octs.count(',')
    step = 7 * o + LET.index(up); alt = acc.count('^') - acc.count('_')
    midi = 12 * o + SEMI[LET.index(up)] + alt + s
    step += d
    def spell(step):
        o2, li = divmod(step, 7); return midi - (12 * o2 + SEMI[li])
    a = spell(step)
    if a > 1: step += 1; a = spell(step)
    elif a < -1: step -= 1; a = spell(step)
    # avoid B#, E#, Cb, Fb
    li = step % 7
    if a == 1 and li in (2, 6): step += 1; a = 0
    if a == -1 and li in (0, 3): step -= 1; a = 0
    o2, li = divmod(step, 7); L = LET[li]
    accs = {0: '', 1: '^', -1: '_', 2: '^^', -2: '__'}[a]
    if o2 >= 5: return accs + L.lower() + "'" * (o2 - 5)
    return accs + L + ',' * (4 - o2)
def transpose(line, iv):
    if iv in ('0', None): return line
    sign = -1 if iv[0] == '-' else 1; d, s = IV[iv.lstrip('+-')]; d *= sign; s *= sign
    m = re.match(r'^\[V:\s*\S+\]', line)
    if not m: return line
    out = m.group(0); i = m.end()
    while i < len(line):
        c = line[i]
        if c == '%': out += line[i:]; break
        if c in '"!':
            j = line.index(c, i + 1); out += line[i:j + 1]; i = j + 1; continue
        f = re.match(r'\[[A-Za-z]:[^\]]*\]', line[i:])
        if f: out += f.group(0); i += f.end(); continue
        n = re.match(r"([\^_]*)([A-Ga-g])([,']*)", line[i:])

    r = subprocess.run(['node', str(ROOT / 'tools/an.js'), str(ROOT / 'out' / f'{stem}.expanded.mw'), str(out), '--quiet'], capture_output=True, text=True)

    text = out.read_text()
    label = re.search(r'^%%label (.*)$', text, re.M).group(1)

The composition notebook

How Bach’s Missing Violin Sonata was written, checked and revised.

An original AI-composed homage in E minor for violin and obbligato keyboard, not a rediscovered work by J. S. Bach. Composed on November 15, 2026, for the first request in the Missing Works voting queue.

This is an edited, high-level account based on the recorded messages, score revisions and test results. It is not a verbatim transcript or a disclosure of private internal reasoning. The musical judgments are analytical. The composing agent inspected notation and synthesised audio buffers; it did not listen to the music, and no person had reviewed it by ear when this page was written.

One motto, four movements

The sonata follows the slow–fast–slow–fast plan of Bach’s sonatas for violin and obbligato keyboard (BWV 1014–1019). The texture is theirs too: three real parts, with the violin and the keyboard’s right hand as equal partners over a bass that takes its share of the themes.

B   E   F♯   G

Up a fourth from the dominant, then two steps to the third of the key.

Every movement begins from this rising figure. The Adagio holds its last note as a suspension. The fugue turns it into running quavers. T .... ation and voice leading, not proof of good music.

  • The checker still reports a few items that were reviewed and kept: dissonances over pedal points near the ends of movements I and II, arpeggiated dominant-ninth chords in the fugue’s dominant bars, and one in the canon’s retransition. In the canon a few sevenths in the following voice leave by leap because the leader’s next bar begins elsewhere.
  • The canon’s harmony is plain. Most bars reach the dominant on their third beat, which keeps the canon workable but may sound predictable.
  • The keyboard is played by a sampled piano to match the site’s violin-sonata category; a harpsichord would balance and articulate differently. The bass is thinner than a continuo player would make it.
  • At about nine and a half minutes the sonata is slightly shorter than the ten to fifteen minutes suggested in the brief.

The composition notebook

How Bernstein’s Missing Quartet was written, checked and revised.

An original AI-composed homage for two violins, viola and cello, not a work by Leonard Bernstein and not endorsed by anyone connected with him. Composed on November 15–16, 2026, for the top-voted request in the Missing Works queue.

This is an edited, high-level account based on the recorded messages, score revisions and test results. It is not a verbatim transcript or a disclosure of private internal reasoning. The musical judgments are analytical. The composing agent inspected notation and synthesised audio buffers; it did not listen to the music, and no person had reviewed the finished quartet by ear when this page was written.

One motto, four movements

Bernstein wrote no string quartet that survives in his catalogue. This one asks what his manner might sound like with four string players: additive metres, stacked fourths and fifths, a big tune, a jazz movement, and themes that come back transformed in later movements.

E   A   D   B

Two rising fourths and a falling third.

Everything grows from this figure. In the first movement it is a 7/8 fanfare and, slowed down, the start of the lyrical second theme. In the scherzo it is the call of a blues riff. In the slow movement its two fourths open the song, and its mirror image (two falling fourths, a rising third) drives the middle section. In the finale it becomes a dance, and the song returns over it.

The quartet lasts about twelve minutes (11:56 in the site’s playback).

I. Allegro con brio

A major · 7/8 (2+2+3) with 5/8 and 3/4 · 106 bars · about 2:49

A two-bar curtain-raiser gives the motto to the violins in octaves and its inversion to viola and cello, then plants two stacks of open fifths a step apart (G, then A). The first theme rides a plucked cello figure: first violin, then viola with a descant above. Played in even eighth notes the motto makes a 5/8 bar, and the transition passes that bar up through all four instruments before slipping a half step off course (A flat, B flat) and landing on C.

The second theme (C major, 3/4, slower) is the motto’s two fourths sung slowly. The viola has it first, over a swaying pizzicato; the first violin repeats it with the second violin in thirds and sixths.

The development is a fugato on the first theme, with entries rising by fifths. A quiet interlude then tries the two themes against each other, because both begin with the same two fourths, and the climax plays them together at full volume in F. The recapitulation brings the second theme back in A; a short coda ends on an A major chord with an added sixth.

II. Scherzo: Riffs

D minor · 12/8 swing · 70 bars · about 2:20

A twelve-bar minor blues over a plucked walking bass. The call is the motto in swing rhythm; second violin and viola answer in parallel fourths and thirds, with blue notes (A flat, and F sharp against F). The form is laid out like a small-band chart: a head, a written-out solo chorus for the first violin, a chorus in which second violin and viola trade two-bar solos, then a hushed fugato whose subject is the motto with a blues tail, answered a fifth higher against a counter-line that walks down by step. A stretto over the dominant brings the blues back with the call an octave higher, and the movement ends with a plucked chord of D minor with added sixth and ninth.

III. Andante con tenerezza

F major · 5/4 (3+2), middle section in 3/4 · 49 bars · about 4:07

The song opens with the motto’s two rising fourths (C, F, B flat) and falls a third. Its eight bars include a Lydian B natural near the end and close through the minor subdominant. The second violin sings it first over a rocking viola; the first violin repeats it with a viola counter-melody.

The middle section turns the motto upside down and passes it upward from viola to second violin to first violin to cello while the harmony falls by fifths (D minor, G minor, C minor, F minor, B flat minor). At the climax the song’s opening returns in the minor over a dominant pedal and turns to the major within two bars. The song then continues quietly, and the cello sings all of it once more with the viola plucking the bass.

IV. Finale: Allegro giocoso

A major · 6/8 against 3/4, with two bars of 7/8 · 132 bars · about 2:39

A rondo. The refrain is the motto as a dance in which 6/8 bars alternate with bars of three quarter notes; while the tune is in one grouping the accompaniment claps the other. The first episode (C major) sets the slow movement’s song in long notes over plucked strings, first in the first violin, then in the viola with a descant. The second episode is a fugato in F sharp minor on the refrain, each entry against a counter-line that crosses its rhythm; it climbs back through two bars of the first movement’s 7/8 theme. In the coda the violins play the song broadly over the dance, the first movement’s curtain-raiser returns, and the last cadence steps F, G, A.

Influences, and what is not quoted

  • No melody is quoted from Bernstein or anyone else. The only quotations are of this quartet’s own themes in later movements.
  • The motto was chosen to stay clear of his best-known melodic signatures: it does not use the rising tritone that resolves up a half step (“Maria”, “Cool”), and the slow movement’s song does not open with the rising seventh of “Somewhere”.
  • Additive and changing metres (7/8, 5/8, 5/4) follow the general manner of the Candide overture, the Chichester Psalms and the Serenade. Stacks of fourths and fifths, a flat seventh degree moving to the tonic, and added sixths and ninths are common to Bernstein and to Copland.
  • The scherzo’s plan of riffs plus a quiet jazz fugue is modelled on the idea of Prelude, Fugue and Riffs and of the “Cool” fugue in West Side Story. The subject, counter-line and blues choruses are new.
  • The finale’s alternation of 6/8 and 3/4 is the huapango rhythm Bernstein used in “America”. It is a traditional rhythm; the tune here is new.
  • Bringing a slow movement’s tune back at the end of a finale over faster music is a device he used on the stage and in concert works; the same is true of many other composers.

How it was written and revised

  • Each movement was written in a private source format in which every note carries its sounding pitch; a compiler writes the ABC notation with the accidentals a reader expects. Recapitulations and rondo returns are generated from the same blocks, transposed by interval where needed.
  • Eight playable draft revisions were published during the work, starting with the first fourteen bars. They remain available from the draft page.
  • First drafts of the four movements came to just under ten minutes. The revision pass added new music rather than repeats: an interlude in the first movement’s development and the viola’s statement of the second theme in its recapitulation; a chorus of traded solos in the scherzo; a last strophe for the cello in the slow movement; a longer coda in the finale. Tempos of the scherzo and slow movement were eased slightly.
  • Things the checks caught and that were fixed before publication: the very first sketch had the three upper parts an octave too high; a metre change written at the start of a line was mis-timed by the notation library; a five-eighth rest could not be notated as one symbol; in the finale an F sharp was missing from two viola bars; and about fo [… 3323 more characters of output not shown]
